author: Andrew Gelman
text: An important aspect of mixture modeling is the selection of the number of mixture components In this paper we discuss the Bayes factor as a selection tool The discussion will focus on two aspects computation of the Bayes factor and prior sensitivity For the computation we propose a variant of Chibs estimator that accounts for the nonidentifiability of the mixture components To reduce the prior sensitivity of the Bayes factor we propose to extend the model with a hyperprior We further discuss the use of posterior predictive checks for examining the fit of the model The ideas are illustrated by means of a psychiatric diagnosis example

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Title Posterior Predictive Assessment Of Model Fitness Via Realized DiscrepanciesAbstract In this paper we introduce a novel framework for evaluating model fitness through the lens of posterior predictive checks focusing on realized discrepancies as a key metric By leveraging the power of Bayesian inference we perform posterior predictive sampling to generate synthetic datasets that reflect the uncertainty encapsulated in the model We then define realized discrepancies as the difference between observed data and predicted data enabling a comprehensive assessment of model adequacy and robustness Our methodology is illustrated using both simulated and realworld datasets showcasing its ability to identify potential shortcomings in model assumptions and fit Through extensive simulation studies and case applications we demonstrate the effectiveness of realized discrepancies in revealing systematic biases and informing model selection processes This work contributes to the growing body of literature on Bayesian diagnostics by providing a practical tool for researchers to critically evaluate their statistical models ultimately leading to improved predictive accuracy and decisionmaking

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for conducting diagnostic checks in discrete data regression models through the application of posterior predictive simulations We investigate the efficacy of these simulations in assessing model fit and identifying potential model misspecifications in a variety of common discrete data scenarios including binary count and ordinal outcomes By leveraging Bayesian methodologies we generate posterior predictive distributions that allow us to compare observed data against predicted values enabling a robust evaluation of model adequacy A series of diagnostic tools such as predictive checks residual analysis and goodnessoffit measures are introduced and applied to both simulated datasets and realworld examples Our findings demonstrate that posterior predictive simulations not only provide substantial insights into the reliability of discrete regression models but also facilitate informed decisions in model selection and refinement processes Ultimately this work underscores the importance of incorporating rigorous diagnostic techniques in the analysis of discrete data promoting more accurate and interpretable statistical inferences

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper investigates the phenomenon of incumbency advantage in electoral contexts through the lens of a beforeafter study design We employ a robust statistical framework to estimate the incumbency effect on electoral outcomes analyzing data from a series of electoral cycles across various jurisdictions Our methodology incorporates both fixed and random effects models to account for unobserved heterogeneity and temporal trends We delve into the variability of incumbency advantage across different political environments and demographic settings providing insights into factors that mediate this advantage The findings highlight significant variations in incumbency effects contingent on electoral competitiveness district characteristics and candidate attributes Additionally we discuss the implications of our results for electoral strategy and political science theory ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of incumbency dynamics in democratic elections By illuminating the nuances of incumbency advantage and its variations our study serves as a vital resource for policymakers political analysts and scholars alike paving the way for future research in this domain

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper considers Bayesian counterparts of the classical tests for goodness of fit and their use in judging the fit of a single Bayesian model to the observed data We focus on posterior predictive assessment in a framework that also includes conditioning on auxiliary statistics The Bayesian formulation facilitates the construction and calculation of a meaningful reference distribution not only for any classical statistic but also for any parameterdependent statistic or discrepancy The latter allows us to propose the realized discrepancy assessment of model fitness which directly measures the true discrepancy between data and the posited model for any aspect of the model which we want to explore The computation required for the realized discrepancy assessment is a straightforward byproduct of the posterior simulation used for the original Bayesian analysis We illustrate with three applied examples The first example which serves mainly to motivate the work illustrates the difficulty of classical tests in assessing the fitness of a Poisson model to a positron emission tomography image that is constrained to be nonnegative The second and third examples illustrate the details of the posterior predictive approach in two problems estimation in a model with inequality constraints on the parameters and estimation in a mixture model In all three examples standard test statistics either a chi or a likelihood ratio are not pivotal the difficulty is not just how to compute the reference distribution for the test but that in the classical framework no such distribution exists independent of the unknown model parameters

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Progress in statistical computation often leads to advances in statistical modeling For example it is surprisingly common that an existing model is reparameterized solely for computational purposes but then this new configuration motivates a new family of models that is useful in applied statistics One reason why this phenomenon may not have been noticed in statistics is that reparameterizations do not change the likelihood In a Bayesian framework however a transformation of parameters typically suggests a new family of prior distributions We discuss examples in censored and truncated data mixture modeling multivariate imputation stochastic processes and multilevel models

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Model checking with discrete data regressions can be difficult because the usual methods such as residual plots have complicated reference distributions that depend on the parameters in the model Posterior predictive checks have been proposed as a Bayesian way to average the results of goodnessoffit tests in the presence of uncertainty in estimation of the parameters We try this approach using a variety of discrepancy variables for generalized linear models fitted to a historical data set on behavioural learning We then discuss the general applicability of our findings in the context of a recent applied example on which we have worked We find that the following discrepancy variables work well in the sense of being easy to interpret and sensitive to important model failures structured displays of the entire data set general discrepancy variables based on plots of binned or smoothed residuals versus predictors and specific discrepancy variables created on the basis of the particular concerns arising in an application Plots of binned residuals are especially easy to use because their predictive distributions under the model are sufficiently simple that model checks can often be made implicitly The following discrepancy variables did not work well scatterplots of latent residuals defined from an underlying continuous model and quantilequantile plots of these residuals

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Incumbency advantage is one of the most widely studied features in American legislative elections In this article we construct and implement an estimate that allows incumbency advantage to vary between individual incumbents This model predicts that openseat elections will be less variable than those with incumbents running an observed empirical pattern that is not explained by previous models We apply our method to the US House of Representatives in the twentieth century Our estimate of the overall pattern of incumbency advantage over time is similar to previous estimates although slightly lower and we also find a pattern of increasing variation More generally our multilevel model represents a new method for estimating effects in beforeafter studies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we propose a comprehensive Bayesian framework for the selection and testing of mixture models which are widely used in various fields including finance biology and social sciences to describe heterogeneous data We address the inherent complexity of mixture models arising from their latent structures and the challenge of identifying the optimal number of components and their corresponding distributions Our approach integrates Bayesian model selection techniques such as the deviance information criterion DIC and the Bayesian pvalue alongside posterior predictive checks to assess model fit We employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods to sample from the posterior distribution enabling robust estimation of model parameters Through extensive simulations and real data applications we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately selecting and validating mixture models while controlling for overfitting and model uncertainty The results indicate that our Bayesian approach enhances the interpretability and reliability of mixture model analyses offering a significant contribution to the field of statistical modeling We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings and potential directions for future research

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we introduce an innovative approach to improving the efficiency of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo HMC sampling through the adaptive adjustment of path lengths in the NoUTurn Sampler NUTS framework Traditional HMC methods often suffer from suboptimal performance due to fixed or heuristically chosen path lengths which can lead to inefficient exploration of complex posterior distributions Our proposed method employs an adaptive strategy that dynamically tunes path lengths based on realtime feedback from trajectory properties enabling the sampler to avoid unnecessary retracing of paths while effectively balancing exploration and exploitation We analyze the theoretical underpinnings of our adaptive mechanism highlighting its convergence properties and robustness across various statistical models Empirical evaluations demonstrate significant improvements in sampling speed and accuracy on benchmark datasets particularly in highdimensional spaces Our work establishes a novel contribution to the adaptive functionality of NUTS paving the way for more efficient Bayesian inference in challenging computational scenarios

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Posterior predictive pvalues do not in general have uniform distributions under the null hypothesis except in the special case of ancillary test variables but instead tend to have distributions more concentrated near From different perspectives such nonuniform distributions have been portrayed as desirable as reflecting an ability of vague prior distributions to nonetheless yield accurate posterior predictions or undesirable as making it more difficult to reject a false model We explore this tension through two simple normaldistribution examples In one example we argue that the low power of the posterior predictive check is desirable from a statistical perspective in the other the posterior predictive check seems inappropriate Our conclusion is that the relevance of the pvalue depends on the applied context a point which ironically can be seen even in these two toy examples

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we explore the concept of Bayesian modelbuilding through a theoretical lens emphasizing the role of pure thought in developing statistical models that align with Bayesian principles We present a framework that allows statisticians to construct probabilistic models based on intuitive reasoning and philosophical foundations rather than solely on empirical data Our approach outlines key principles that guide the modelbuilding process including the importance of prior beliefs the formulation of likelihood functions and the integration of expert knowledge Through a series of illustrative examples we demonstrate how these principles can be applied to various statistical challenges ranging from simple linear models to complex hierarchical structures By bridging the gap between theoretical underpinnings and practical applications this paper aims to foster a deeper understanding of Bayesian methodology and encourage statisticians to engage in modelbuilding that transcends traditional datadriven constraints Ultimately we argue that incorporating cognitive frameworks can enhance the richness and flexibility of Bayesian inference leading to more robust and interpretable models

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In the realm of modern data science exploratory data analysis EDA serves as a pivotal phase in understanding interpreting and preparing data for complex statistical models This paper investigates advanced EDA techniques specifically tailored for complex models which often include multivariate hierarchical and nonlinear structures that traditional EDA methods may inadequately address We present a comprehensive framework that integrates interactive visualization tools dimension reduction methods and feature extraction techniques to enhance the descriptive analysis of highdimensional datasets Through systematic case studies involving simulated and realworld datasets we illustrate the efficacy of our framework in uncovering intricate patterns detecting anomalies and informing model selection processes The findings highlight the importance of iterative exploration and the necessity of robust visualization techniques in guiding the modeling strategy ultimately contributing to improved model performance and interpretability This work advocates for a paradigm shift in EDA emphasizing its critical role in laying the groundwork for successful applications of complex modeling approaches in various fields including social sciences finance and biological research

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In applications statistical models are often restricted to what produces reasonable estimates based on the dat a at hand In many cases however the principles that allow a model to be restricted can be derived theoretically in the absence of any data and with minimal applied contert We illustrate this point with three wellknown theoretical examples from spatial statistics and time series First we show that an autoregressive model for local average violates a principle of invariance under scaling Second we show how the Bayesian estimate of a strictlyincreasing time series using a uniform prior distribution depends on the scale of estimation Third we interpret local smoothing of spatial lattice data as Bayesian estimation and show why uniform local smoothing does not make sense In various forms the results presented here have been derived in previous work our contribution is to draw out some principles that can be derived theoretically even though in the past they may have been presented in detail in the context of specific examples

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In Bayesian hypothesis testing posterior pvalues serve as crucial tools for assessing evidence against null hypotheses However the interpretation and utility of posterior pvalues can be challenging especially when their distributions deviate significantly from uniformity This paper presents two simple yet illustrative examples that highlight the nuances of posterior pvalues in nonstandard contexts The first example examines a case where the posterior distribution is skewed illustrating how this skewness impacts the validity of the posterior pvalue as a measure of evidence The second example explores a scenario involving multimodal posterior distributions demonstrating the potential for misleading conclusions when relying exclusively on posterior pvalues Through these examples we aim to foster a deeper understanding of the limitations and appropriate applications of posterior pvalues emphasizing the necessity of combined interpretative strategies when dealing with diverse posterior landscapes The findings underscore the importance of careful consideration when evaluating posterior pvalues contributing to a more nuanced approach in Bayesian analysis

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo HMC is a Markov chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithm that avoids the random walk behavior and sensitivity to correlated parameters that plague many MCMC methods by taking a series of steps informed by firstorder gradient information These features allow it to converge to highdimensional target distributions much more quickly than simpler methods such as random walk Metropolis or Gibbs sampling However HMCs performance is highly sensitive to two userspecified parameters a step size is an element of and a desired number of steps L In particular if L is too small then the algorithm exhibits undesirable random walk behavior while if L is too large the algorithm wastes computation We introduce the NoUTurn Sampler NUTS an extension to HMC that eliminates the need to set a number of steps L NUTS uses a recursive algorithm to build a set of likely candidate points that spans a wide swath of the target distribution stopping automatically when it starts to double back and retrace its steps Empirically NUTS performs at least as efficiently as and sometimes more efficiently than a well tuned standard HMC method without requiring user intervention or costly tuning runs We also derive a method for adapting the step size parameter is an element of on the fly based on primaldual averaging NUTS can thus be used with no handtuning at all making it suitable for applications such as BUGSstyle automatic inference engines that require efficient turnkey samplers

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Exploratory and confirmatory data analysis can both be viewed as methods for comparing observed data to what Would be obtained tinder an implicit or explicit statistical model For example many of Tukeys methods can be interpreted as checks against hypothetical linear models and Poisson distributions In more complex situations Bayesian methods can be useful for constructing reference distributions for various plots that are useful in exploratory data analysis This article proposes an approach to unify exploratory data analysis with more formal statistical methods based on probability models These ideas are developed in the context of examples front fields including psychology medicine and social science

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Ecological regression models are widely employed in the field of ecology to analyze relationships between variables at a group or population level often based on aggregate data However the validity of insights derived from these models is heavily dependent on the underlying assumptions and the robustness of model checking procedures This paper examines the critical assumptions inherent in ecological regression frameworks such as the linearity independence and homoscedasticity of residuals while also emphasizing the importance of ecological fallacy and the modifiable areal unit problem We present a comprehensive overview of model checking techniques including graphical diagnostic methods and statistical tests aimed at assessing the adequacy of fitted models Additionally we illustrate the implications of assumption violations through simulated datasets and realworld case studies reflecting on how misinterpretations can arise when assumptions are overlooked Our findings underscore the necessity of rigorous model evaluation to enhance the credibility and applicability of ecological regression analyses in environmental research The paper concludes with practical recommendations for ecologists and statisticians to refine their modeling approaches and ensure sound inferential conclusions

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Ecological regression is based on assumptions that are untestable from aggregate data However these assumptions seem more questionable in some applications than in others There has been some research on implicit models of individual data underlying aggregate ecological regression modelling We discuss ways in which these implicit models can be checked from aggregate data We also explore the differences in applications of ecological regressions in two examples estimating the effect of radon on lung cancer in the United States and estimating voting patterns for different ethnic groups in New York City

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we explore the intricacies of parameterization and its implications for Bayesian modeling in statistical inference Parameterization serves as a critical foundation for the development of robust models influencing both the interpretability of the results and the efficiency of the estimation process We discuss various approaches to parameterization including conventional and hierarchical strategies and their impact on computational feasibility and model performance Utilizing a series of simulations and realworld datasets we demonstrate how different parameterization frameworks affect the convergence of Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC algorithms and the accuracy of posterior estimates Additionally we introduce a novel Bayesian modeling framework that incorporates adaptive parameterization techniques to enhance model flexibility and predictive power Through comparative analysis we highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional methods Our findings offer valuable insights for statisticians and data scientists emphasizing the importance of careful parameterization in the broader context of Bayesian analysis The paper concludes with practical recommendations for implementing effective parameterization strategies in future Bayesian modeling endeavors

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this study we investigate the probabilistic underpinnings of facial perception of emotions employing advanced statistical methodologies to analyze how various facial features influence the recognition and interpretation of emotional states Leveraging a dataset comprising thousands of facial images annotated with emotional labels we apply a Bayesian framework to model the relationships between specific facial features such as eye shape mouth curvature and brow position and perceived emotions including happiness sadness anger and surprise Our findings reveal nuanced patterns in featureemotion associations highlighting the probabilistic nature of emotion recognition and the variability in individual perceivers interpretations Additionally we explore the impact of demographic factors such as age and cultural background on facial emotion perception underscoring how context can modulate probabilistic interpretations of facial expressions This research contributes to the fields of psychology computer vision and affective computing by offering a robust statistical foundation for understanding the complexities of emotion recognition through facial characteristics Furthermore the insights garnered from this analysis have practical implications for applications in mental health diagnostics humancomputer interaction and automated emotion recognition systems

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We describe a general approach using Bayesian analysis for the estimation of parameters in physiological pharmacokinetic models The chief statistical difficulty in estimation with these models is that any physiological model that is even approximately realistic will have a large number ofparameters often comparable to the number of observations in a typical pharmacokinetic experiment eg measurements and parameters for each subject In addition the parameters are generally poorly identified akin to the wellknown illconditioned problem of estimating a mixture of declining exponentials Our modeling includes a hierarchical population modeling which allows partial pooling of information among different experimental subjects b a pharmacokinetic model including compartments for wellperfused tissues poorly perfused tissues fat and the liver and c informative prior distributions for population parameters which is possible because the parameters represent real physiological variables We discuss how to estimate the models using Bayesian posterior simulation a method that automatically includes the uncertainty inherent in estimating such a large number of parameters We also discuss how to check model fit and sensitivity to the prior distribution using posterior predictive simulation We illustrate the application to the toxicokinetics of tetrachloroethylene perchloroethylene PERC the problem that motivated this work

author: Andrew Gelman
text: One of the longest running questions that has been regularly included in US national public opinion polls is Are you in favor of the death penalty for persons convicted of murder Because the death penalty is governed by state laws rather than federal laws it is of special interest to know how public opinion varies by state and how it has changed over time within each state We combine dozens of national polls taken over a year span and fit a Bayesian multilevel logistic regression model to estimate support for the death penalty as a function of the year the state state level variables and various individual level demographic variables Among our findings were that support levels in northeastern and southern states have moved in opposite directions over the past years support among blacks has decreased relative to nonblacks but at slightly different rates for men and women and support among some education groups varies widely by region Throughout the paper we highlight the use of a variety of analytical and graphical tools for model understanding including average predictive comparisons finite population contrasts for overparameterized models and graphical summaries of posterior distributions of group level variance parameters

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We derive conditions under which a set of conditional and marginal probability distributions will uniquely specify an allpositive joint distribution Our theoretical result may yield insights into the construction and simulation of multivariate probability models

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In the realm of statistical analysis handling missing data is a critical concern that can significantly impact the validity of results This paper investigates the stationary distribution of iterative imputations a widely used technique in the context of missing data We begin by formulating a rigorous mathematical framework for iterative imputation processes highlighting the convergence properties and stability of the imputed data distributions Using Markov chain theory we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a stationary distribution under various imputation algorithms such as Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations MICE and Bayesian methods Through a series of simulations we explore the convergence behavior and empirical distributions generated through iterative imputations revealing insights into the bias and variability of estimates stemming from nonstationary behaviors Our findings underscore the importance of assessing convergence in practical applications of imputation methods providing statisticians with guidelines to enhance the robustness of their analyses in the presence of incomplete data The results extend the theoretical understanding of iterative imputation processes and offer practical implications for improving imputation strategies in applied statistical research

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Iterative imputation in which variables are imputed one at a time conditional on all the others is a popular technique that can be convenient and flexible as it replaces a potentially difficult multivariate modelling problem with relatively simple univariate regressions In this paper we begin to characterize the stationary distributions of iterative imputations and their statistical properties accounting for the conditional models being iteratively estimated from data rather than being prespecified When the families of conditional models are compatible we provide sufficient conditions under which the imputation distribution converges in total variation to the posterior distribution of a Bayesian model When the conditional models are incompatible but valid we show that the combined imputation estimator is consistent

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In recent years public opinion regarding the death penalty in the United States has become a focal point of both legal and sociopolitical discourse This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of state and demographic trends in public opinion on the death penalty using hierarchical modeling techniques By synthesizing data from a variety of national surveys we develop a multilevel model that accounts for variability in opinions across states while incorporating demographic factors such as age race gender and education level Our approach allows for the estimation of both individuallevel influences and statespecific effects providing insights into how regional contexts shape public attitudes toward capital punishment We identify significant trends over time noting shifts in public sentiment that correlate with changes in legal practices and societal norms Furthermore our findings highlight the interaction between demographic variables and geographic location revealing nuanced patterns of support and opposition to the death penalty across different groups This study contributes to the understanding of public opinion dynamics and offers implications for policymakers legal practitioners and advocates involved in the ongoing debate surrounding capital punishment in the United States

author: Andrew Gelman
text: According to the hypothesis of configural encoding the spatial relationships between the parts of the face function as an additional source of information in the facial perception of emotions The paper analyses experimental data on the perception of emotion to investigate whether there is evidence for configural encoding in the processing of facial expressions It is argued that analysis with a probabilistic feature model has several advantages that are not implied by for example a generalized linear modelling approach First the probabilistic feature model allows us to extract empirically the facial features that are relevant in processing the face rather than focusing on the features that were manipulated in the experiment Second the probabilistic feature model allows a direct test of the hypothesis of configural encoding as it explicitly formalizes a mechanism for the way in which information about separate facial features is combined in processing the face Third the model allows us to account for a complex data structure while still yielding parameters that have a straightforward interpretation

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Exploratory data analysis EDA and Bayesian inference or more generally complex statistical modelingwhich are generally considered as unrelated statistical paradigmscan be particularly effective in combination In this paper we present a Bayesian framework for EDA based on posterior predictive checks We explain how posterior predictive simulations can be used to create reference distributions for EDA graphs and how this approach resolves some theoretical problems in Bayesian data analysis We show how the generalization of Bayesian inference to include replicated data yrep and replicated parameters thetarep follows a long tradition of generalizations in Bayesian theory On the theoretical level we present a predictive Bayesian formulation of goodnessoffit testing distinguishing between pvalues posterior probabilities that specified antisymmetric discrepancy measures will exceed and uvalues data summaries with uniform sampling distributions We explain that pvalues unlike uvalues are Bayesian probability statements in that they condition on observed data Having reviewed the general theoretical framework we discuss the implications for statistical graphics and exploratory data analysis with the goal being to unify exploratory data analysis with more formal statistical methods based on probability models We interpret various graphical displays as posterior predictive checks and discuss how Bayesian inference can be used to determine reference distributions The goal of this work is not to downgrade descriptive statistics or to suggest they be replaced by Bayesian modeling but rather to suggest how exploratory data analysis fits into the probabilitymodeling paradigm We conclude with a discussion of the implications for practical Bayesian inference In particular we anticipate that Bayesian software can be generalized to draw simulations of replicated data and parameters from their posterior predictive distribution and these can in turn be used to calibrate EDA graphs

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn this paper we explore the characterization of joint probability distributions through the lens of conditional probabilities We begin by establishing a foundational theoretical framework that links joint distributions to their conditional counterparts employing key concepts from measure theory and probability By examining various examples and counterexamples we illustrate the implications of conditional independence and dependence on the shape and behavior of joint distributions We then propose a novel methodology for reconstructing joint distributions using a finite set of conditional probabilities which we demonstrate through both synthetic and realworld datasets Our results show that this approach not only provides insights into the structure of complex probabilistic models but also enhances the efficiency of Bayesian inference processes Finally we discuss the practical applications of our findings in fields such as machine learning epidemiology and data science highlighting the relevance of conditional distributions in modern statistical analysis This work contributes to the ongoing discourse on the interplay between conditional and joint distributions offering new avenues for research and application in probabilistic modeling

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn the realm of pharmacokinetics understanding the variability in drug response among individuals is crucial for optimizing therapeutic strategies This paper presents a comprehensive approach to physiological pharmacokinetic analysis by integrating population modeling with informative prior distributions We develop a hierarchical modeling framework that leverages rich clinical data to capture interindividual variability in drug absorption distribution metabolism and elimination processes Informative priors derived from previous studies and physiological benchmarks are employed to enhance parameter estimation and improve model robustness Utilizing a Bayesian inference framework we demonstrate how this approach facilitates the identification of demographic and physiological covariates that significantly influence pharmacokinetic parameters Our results indicate that the combination of population modeling with informative priors yields more accurate predictions of drug behavior across diverse patient populations The findings underscore the potential for this methodology to inform personalized medicine by enabling tailored dosing strategies that account for individual variability ultimately improving treatment outcomes in clinical settings

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn statistical analysis the presence of missing or latent data can compromise the validity of model diagnostics and result interpretation Traditional approaches to model checking often assume complete data neglecting the uncertainty introduced by missing values This paper introduces a novel framework for multiple imputation specifically tailored for model checking utilizing completeddata plots to assess model fit while explicitly accounting for missingness and latent structure We develop a systematic procedure for generating multiple imputed datasets allowing for comprehensive visualizations that reflect the variability due to imputation Our methodology enhances the robustness of model diagnostics by integrating uncertainty from missing data into graphical representations thereby providing a more nuanced understanding of model performance We illustrate our approach through simulations and real data applications demonstrating its efficacy in unveiling underlying patterns and ensuring reliable conclusions in the presence of incomplete information This work represents a significant advancement in the integration of multiple imputation techniques with model checking promoting rigorous statistical practices in the analysis of complex datasets

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractExploratory Data Analysis EDA plays a pivotal role in the initial stages of datadriven research facilitating insights through visual and quantitative methods This paper proposes a novel Bayesian framework for EDA that integrates goodnessoffit testing to enhance the interpretation and analysis of complex datasets Our approach leverages Bayesian principles to quantify uncertainty allowing researchers to derive probabilistic insights into data distributions and model fit We introduce several Bayesian EDA techniques including posterior predictive checks Bayesian model comparison and credibility intervals which offer robust alternatives to traditional frequentist methods Through simulations and realworld examples we demonstrate that our Bayesian formulation not only provides clearer insights into data characteristics but also improves the reliability of goodnessoffit assessments This work advocates for a paradigm shift in EDA practices by incorporating Bayesian methods fostering a more nuanced understanding of data and models in statistical analysis

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In problems with missing or latent data a standard approach is to first impute the unobserved data then perform all statistical analyses on the completed datasetcorresponding to the observed data and imputed unobserved datausing standard procedures for completedata inference Here we extend this approach to model checking by demonstrating the advantages of the use of completeddata model diagnostics on imputed completed datasets The approach is set in the theoretical framework of Bayesian posterior predictive checks but as with missingdata imputation our methods of missingdata model checking can also be interpreted as predictive inference in a nonBayesian context We consider the graphical diagnostics within this framework Advantages of the completeddata approach include One can often check model fit in terms of quantities that are of key substantive interest in a natural way which is not always possible using observed data alone In problems with missing data checks may be devised that do net require to model the missingness or inclusion mechanism the latter is useful for the analysis of ignorable but unknown data collection mechanisms such as are often assumed in the analysis of sample surveys and observational studies In many problems with latent data it is possible to check qualitative features of the model for example independence of two variables that can be naturally formalized with the help of the latent data We illustrate with several applied examples

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Practical Bayesian data analysis involves manipulating and summarizing simulations from the posterior distribution of the unknown parameters By manipulation we mean computing posterior distributions of functions of the unknowns and generating posterior predictive distributions The results need to be summarized both numerically and graphically We introduce and implement in R an objectoriented programming paradigm based on a random variable object type that is implicitly represented by simulations This makes it possible to define vector and array objects that may contain both random and deterministic quantities and syntax rules that allow to treat these objects like any numeric vectors or arrays providing a solution to various problems encountered in Bayesian computing involving posterior simulations We illustrate the use of this new programming environment with examples of Bayesian computing demonstrating missingvalue imputation nonlinear summary of regression predictions and posterior predictive checking

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Researchers sometimes argue that statisticians have little to contribute when few realizations of the process being estimated are observed We show that this argument is incorrect even in the extreme situation of estimating the probabilities of events so rare that they have never occurred We show how statistical forecasting models allow us to use empirical data to improve inferences about the probabilities of these events Our application is estimating the probability that your vote will be decisive in a US presidential election a problem that has been studied by political scientists for more than two decades The exact value of this probability is of only minor interest but the number has important implications for understanding the optimal allocation of campaign resources whether states and voter groups receive their fair share of attention from prospective presidents and how formal rational choice models of voter behavior might be able to explain why people vote at all We show how the probability of a decisive vote can be estimated empirically from statelevel forecasts of the presidential election and illustrate with the example of Based on generalizations of standard political science forecasting models we estimate the prospective probability of a single vote being decisive as about in million for close national elections such as varying by about a factor of among states Our results support the argument that subjective probabilities of many types are best obtained through empirically based statistical prediction models rather than solely through mathematical reasoning We discuss the implications of our findings for the types of decision analyses used in public choice studies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Title Estimating The Probability Of Events That Have Never Occurred When Is Your Vote Decisive In the realm of decision theory and electoral participation understanding the likelihood of events that have never previously transpired poses significant challenges for statisticians and voters alike This paper introduces a novel framework for estimating the probability of decisiveness in voting scenarios particularly in elections where historical data is sparse or nonexistent We employ advanced statistical techniques including Bayesian inference and nonparametric methods to evaluate the potential impact of an individuals vote in various electoral systems Through simulations and case studies we explore factors such as voter turnout margin of victory and system dynamics to derive a quantitative measure of decisiveness Our findings reveal crucial insights into when a single vote can alter the outcome providing voters with a clearer understanding of their influence in democratic processes This research not only enriches the theoretical landscape of decisionmaking under uncertainty but also offers practical implications for civic engagement and electoral strategy

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We review weighting adjustment methods for panel attrition and suggest approaches for incorporating design variables such as strata clusters and baseline sample weights Design information can typically be included in attrition analysis using multilevel models or decision tree methods such as the chisquare automatic interaction detection algorithm We use simulation to show that these weighting approaches can effectively reduce bias in the survey estimates that would occur from omitting the effect of design factors on attrition while keeping the resulted weights stable We provide a stepbystep illustration on creating weighting adjustments for panel attrition in the Galveston Bay Recovery Study a survey of residents in a community following a disaster and provide suggestions to analysts in decisionmaking about weighting approaches Copyright c John Wiley Sons Ltd

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We present a method of analyzing a series of independent crosssectional surveys in which some questions are not answered in some surveys and some respondents do not answer some of the questions posed The method is also applicable to a single survey in which different questions are asked or different sampling methods are used in different strata or clusters Our method involves multiply imputing the missing items and questions by adding to existing methods of imputation designed for single surveys a hierarchical regression model that allows covariates at the individual and survey levels Information from survey weights is exploited by including in the analysis the variables on which the weights were based and then reweighting individual responses observed and imputed to estimate population quantities We also develop diagnostics for checking the fit of the imputation model based on comparing imputed data to nonimputed data We illustrate with the example that motivated this project a study of preelection public opinion polls in which not all the questions of interest are asked in all the surveys so that it is infeasible to impute within each survey separately

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We propose a new prior distribution for classical nonhierarchical logistic regression models constructed by first scaling all nonbinary variables to have mean and standard deviation and then placing independent Studentt prior distributions on the coefficients As a default choice we recommend the Cauchy distribution with center and scale which in the simplest setting is a longertailed version of the distribution attained by assuming onehalf additional success and onehalf additional failure in a logistic regression Crossvalidation on a corpus of datasets shows the Cauchy class of prior distributions to outperform existing implementations of Gaussian and Laplace priors We recommend this prior distribution as a default choice for routine applied use It has the advantage of always giving answers even when there is complete separation in logistic regression a common problem even when the sample size is large and the number of predictors is small and also automatically applying more shrinkage to higherorder interactions This can be useful in routine data analysis as well as in automated procedures such as chained equations for missingdata imputation We implement a procedure to fit generalized linear models in R with the Studentt prior distribution by incorporating an approximate EM algorithm into the usual iteratively weighted least squares We illustrate with several applications including a series of logistic regressions predicting voting preferences a small bioassay experiment and an imputation model for a public health data set

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Panel surveys are crucial for longitudinal research but they often face challenges due to panel attrition which can bias results if not properly addressed This paper presents a novel approach to incorporate the sampling design in weighting adjustments for panel attrition enhancing the representativeness of survey estimates Our methodology involves a duallayer weighting strategy that accounts for both the initial sample design and the observed attrition patterns over time We utilize a Bayesian framework to estimate the attrition weights integrating auxiliary data to improve precision Our findings based on simulations and empirical applications demonstrate that incorporating the sampling design significantly mitigates bias and reduces variance in parameter estimates compared to traditional weighting methods This approach not only improves the validity of longitudinal analyses but also provides insights into the mechanisms behind attrition allowing researchers to better understand sample dynamics We conclude that adopting this comprehensive weighting adjustment framework offers a robust solution for addressing the complexities of panel attrition in social science research

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We analyze the effects of redistricting as revealed in the votes received by the Democratic and Republican candidates for state legislature We develop measures of partisan bias and the responsiveness of the composition of the legislature to changes in statewide votes Our statistical model incorporates a mixed hierarchical Bayesian and nonBayesian estimation requiring simulation along the lines of Tanner and Wong This model provides reliable estimates of partisan bias and responsiveness along with measures of their variabilities from only a single year of electoral data This allows one to distinguish systematic changes in the underlying electoral system from typical electiontoelection variability

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Maps of disease rates and other quantities often must contend with variance associated with variable population sizes and low incidence within spatial units These characteristics can lead to substantial statistical noise that can mask underlying spatial variation As Gelman and Price illustrated most conventional mapping methods fail to address this problem and in fact can introduce statistical artefacts mapped quantities can show spatial patterns even when there are no spatial patterns in the underlying parameter of interest Kafadar evaluated the performance of the headbanging algorithm for spatial smoothing Tukey and Tukey Hansen for eliminating small scale variation and preserving edge structure Here we perform a simulation study to investigate the artefacts of maps smoothed by unweighted and weighted headbanging We find substantial artefacts that depend on the spatial structure of the statistical Variation for example the spatial pattern of sample sizes and on the details of the spatial distribution of geographic units The methods used here could readily be adapted to study other spatial smoothers we choose headbanging because i it is an important method used in practice and ii its heavily computational nature is naturally studied using simulation in contrast to the analytical methods used by Gelman and Price Copyright C John Wiley Sons Ltd

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Legislative redistricting plays a critical role in shaping electoral outcomes and influences the political landscape in significant ways This paper presents a comprehensive statistical analysis of the electoral consequences of redistricting utilizing a novel methodological framework that combines geospatial analysis regression modeling and simulation techniques We employ a dataset encompassing electoral results and demographic data from multiple electoral cycles across various jurisdictions allowing for a robust comparison of electoral performance before and after redistricting Our findings reveal that redistricting not only alters the spatial distribution of voters but also leads to significant shifts in party representation and voter turnout We further identify specific redistricting strategies that disproportionately benefit particular political parties providing insights into the mechanisms underlying electoral manipulation By quantifying the impact of redistricting on electoral competitiveness and voter engagement this study contributes to the ongoing debate on electoral integrity and democratic representation offering policymakers and stakeholders actionable insights for future legislative reforms

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we introduce a novel methodology that leverages image and curve registration techniques to enhance the evaluation of the goodness of fit for spatial and temporal predictions in statistical models Traditional metrics for assessing model fit often fall short in capturing the nuanced discrepancies between observed and predicted data particularly in contexts where the data exhibits complex spatial and temporal structures Our proposed framework integrates image registration algorithms with curve fitting approaches to quantify these discrepancies more effectively We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through a series of simulations and realworld case studies across various fields including environmental modeling and epidemiology By aligning spatial and temporal dimensions in a unified framework we provide a robust statistical tool for practitioners enabling more accurate assessments of predictive performance The findings suggest that image and curve registration not only improves the precision of goodnessoffit measurements but also facilitates deeper insights into model behavior ultimately leading to betterinformed decisions based on statistical predictions This work bridges the gap between advanced statistical techniques and practical applications setting a foundation for future research in model evaluation

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn the realm of survey research incomplete data poses significant challenges to accurate inference and decisionmaking This study introduces a novel multiple imputation framework specifically designed for handling nonresponse across multiple surveys where certain key questions remain unasked for subsets of participants We examine the implications of this selective nonresponse on the validity of statistical estimates and the potential biases introduced in subsequent analyses Our method leverages a combination of machine learning algorithms and hierarchical modeling to exploit the structure inherent in multiple datasets enabling the generation of plausible values for missing responses Through a comprehensive simulation study we validate our approach against traditional imputation methods highlighting improvements in estimation accuracy and robustness We further illustrate the practical application of our technique with realworld survey data demonstrating its efficacy in addressing complex patterns of nonresponse The results underscore the importance of advanced imputation methods in enhancing the reliability of survey findings ultimately contributing to more informed policy and research outcomes

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn this paper we present a novel approach for the output assessment of Monte Carlo simulations utilizing the score statistic Monte Carlo methods are widely employed for their flexibility and power in estimating complex statistical models yet the quality and reliability of their outputs are often challenging to evaluate Our proposed methodology leverages the score statistic a key concept in statistical inference to provide a robust framework for assessing the validity of simulation results We establish a theoretical foundation that connects the properties of the score statistic to the convergence behavior of Monte Carlo estimates facilitating a systematic examination of output variability and bias Through a series of simulations across various statistical models we demonstrate how the score statistic can effectively highlight discrepancies in simulation outputs and guide the refinement of sampling strategies Our findings indicate that this approach not only enhances the reliability of output assessments but also offers actionable insights for improving estimation techniques in Monte Carlo simulations This work contributes to the broader field of computational statistics by providing a rigorous tool for practitioners to critically evaluate the outcomes of their Monte Carlo methodologies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Conventional measures of model fit for indexed data eg time series or spatial data summarize errors in y for instance by integrating or summing the squared difference between predicted and measured values over a range of x We propose an approach which recognizes that errors can occur in the xdirection as well Instead of just measuring the difference between the predictions and observations at each site or time we first deform the predictions stretching or compressing along the xdirection or directions so as to improve the agreement between the observations and the deformed predictions Error is then summarized by a the amount of deformation in x and b the remaining difference in y between the data and the deformed predictions ie the residual error in y after the deformation A parameter A controls the tradeoff between a and b so that as lambda infinity no deformation is allowed whereas for lambda the deformation minimizes the errors in y In some applications the deformation itself is of interest because it characterizes the temporal or spatial structure of the errors The optimal deformation can be computed by solving a system of nonlinear partial differential equations or for a unidimensional index by using a dynamic programming algorithm We illustrate the procedure with examples from nonlinear time series and fluid dynamics

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn statistical analysis the presence of missing or latent data can compromise the validity of model diagnostics and result interpretation Traditional approaches to model checking often assume complete data neglecting the uncertainty introduced by missing values This paper introduces a novel framework for multiple imputation specifically tailored for model checking utilizing completeddata plots to assess model fit while explicitly accounting for missingness and latent structure We develop a systematic procedure for generating multiple imputed datasets allowing for comprehensive visualizations that reflect the variability due to imputation Our methodology enhances the robustness of model diagnostics by integrating uncertainty from missing data into graphical representations thereby providing a more nuanced understanding of model performance We illustrate our approach through simulations and real data applications demonstrating its efficacy in unveiling underlying patterns and ensuring reliable conclusions in the presence of incomplete information This work represents a significant advancement in the integration of multiple imputation techniques with model checking promoting rigorous statistical practices in the analysis of complex datasets

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In problems with missing or latent data a standard approach is to first impute the unobserved data then perform all statistical analyses on the completed datasetcorresponding to the observed data and imputed unobserved datausing standard procedures for completedata inference Here we extend this approach to model checking by demonstrating the advantages of the use of completeddata model diagnostics on imputed completed datasets The approach is set in the theoretical framework of Bayesian posterior predictive checks but as with missingdata imputation our methods of missingdata model checking can also be interpreted as predictive inference in a nonBayesian context We consider the graphical diagnostics within this framework Advantages of the completeddata approach include One can often check model fit in terms of quantities that are of key substantive interest in a natural way which is not always possible using observed data alone In problems with missing data checks may be devised that do net require to model the missingness or inclusion mechanism the latter is useful for the analysis of ignorable but unknown data collection mechanisms such as are often assumed in the analysis of sample surveys and observational studies In many problems with latent data it is possible to check qualitative features of the model for example independence of two variables that can be naturally formalized with the help of the latent data We illustrate with several applied examples

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In the fields of biomechanics and sports science accurately quantifying movement patterns is crucial for understanding the effects of specific activities on the human body This paper presents a novel method for quantifying artefacts in mapping techniques specifically through the lens of headbanging a repetitive highimpact movement commonly associated with heavy metal music Traditional mapping methods often struggle with the inherent noise and variability that can obscure true biomechanical signals Our approach employs a robust statistical framework to identify and quantify artefacts arising from both measurement errors and variations in individual performance By applying our method to a series of controlled headbanging trials we demonstrate how artefacts can be systematically categorized and measured resulting in more precise interpretations of motion data We further discuss the implications of this methodology for enhancing the reliability of biomechanical analyses in various contexts Our findings underscore the importance of artefact quantification in mapping methods and provide a valuable tool for researchers aiming to improve data fidelity in dynamic movement studies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In the realm of Bayesian statistics the choice of prior distribution plays a crucial role in shaping the inference of model parameters This paper introduces a weakly informative default prior distribution tailored specifically for logistic and other regression models addressing the need for a balance between informative and noninformative priors We derive the proposed prior based on a systematic analysis of parameter behavior and domain knowledge ensuring robustness across a variety of regression contexts Through extensive simulations and case studies we demonstrate that our default prior effectively stabilizes estimates in scenarios with limited data while still allowing for datadriven contributions to posterior inference We further explore the implications of our prior choice in terms of frequentist coverage rates and predictive performance showing that it outperforms standard noninformative priors in practical applications By providing a readily applicable framework this work aims to enhance Bayesian practitioners toolkit in regression modeling and encourages the thoughtful integration of weakly informative priors in statistical analyses

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In Bayesian data analysis the manipulation and summarization of posterior simulations are crucial for effective inference and decisionmaking This paper introduces a novel framework utilizing Random Variable Objects RVOs to streamline the analysis of posterior samples generated from complex probabilistic models We demonstrate how RVOs can encapsulate the properties and behavior of random variables facilitating enhanced operations such as aggregation transformation and probabilistic querying Through a series of case studies we illustrate the application of RVOs in summarizing key parameters exploring uncertainty and performing model comparisons Our approach offers several advantages including improved computational efficiency and greater flexibility in handling diverse data types and structures We provide a comprehensive set of tools and guidelines for researchers to implement RVOs in their Bayesian workflows ultimately contributing to the development of more accessible and interpretable Bayesian analysis methods The framework is made available in an opensource software package promoting reproducibility and encouraging further innovation in the field

text: We generalize the method proposed by Gelman and Rubin a for monitoring the convergence of iterative simulations by comparing between and within variances of multiple chains in order to obtain a family of tests for convergence We review methods of inference from simulations in older to develop convergencemonitoring summaries that are relevant for the purposes for which the simulations are used We recommend applying a battery of tests for mixing based on the comparison of inferences from individual sequences and from the mixture of sequences Finally we discuss multivariate analogues for assessing convergence of several parameters simultaneously

text: Understanding the social networks that connect individuals to highrisk populations such as those incarcerated is crucial for comprehending the broader implications of crime and rehabilitation This paper explores the unique application of overdispersion in count data to estimate social structures and the density of connections individuals have to people in prison We utilize a dataset comprising selfreported social connections from a diverse sample of respondents analyzing the count of acquaintances known to be incarcerated By employing statistical models that account for overdispersion typified by greater variance than the mean in count data we identify significant patterns and correlations within social networks that traditional models may overlook Our findings reveal not only the prevalence of connections to incarcerated individuals but also how demographic factors and social networks influence these connections The implications of these insights extend to policies regarding criminal justice reform community support programs and the understanding of social capital dynamics Ultimately this study sheds light on the complexity of social structures and their role in shaping individual experiences with the criminal justice system

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Networkssets of objects connected by relationshipsare important in a number of fields The study of networks has long been central to sociology where researchers have attempted to understand the causes and consequences of the structure of relationships in large groups of people Using insight from previous network research Killworth et al and McCarty et al have developed and evaluated a method for estimating the sizes of hardtocount populations using network data collected from a simple random sample of Americans In this article we show how using a multilevel overdispersed Poisson regression model these data also can be used to estimate aspects of social structure in the population Our work goes beyond most previous research on networks by using variation as well as average responses as a source of information We apply our method to the data of McCarty et al and find that Americans vary greatly in their number of acquaintances Further Americans show great variation in propensity to form ties to people in some groups eg males in prison the homeless and American Indians but little variation for other groups eg twins people named Michael or Nicole We also explore other features of these data and consider ways in which survey data can be used to estimate network structure

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we propose an adaptive scaling approach to the Metropolis algorithm a fundamental component of Markov Chain Monte Carlo MCMC methods by introducing a metric based on the expected squared jumped distance ESJD Traditional implementations of the Metropolis algorithm often struggle with tuning the proposal distribution leading to inefficient exploration of the target distribution particularly in highdimensional spaces Our method dynamically adjusts the scale of the proposal distribution in response to the observed samples leveraging the ESJD as an indicator of both local structure and global convergence properties We derive a robust framework that integrates ESJD calculations into the standard Metropolis acceptance criteria enabling selfoptimization of the scaling parameter throughout the sampling process Through extensive simulations and comparative analysis against classic scaling techniques we demonstrate significant improvements in convergence rates and effective sample sizes affirming the efficacy of our adaptive strategy Our results underscore the potential of the ESJDbased scaling method to enhance the performance of MCMC sampling across diverse applications including Bayesian inference and statistical physics

text: In an era characterized by data proliferation and complexity the importance of robust statistical methodologies has never been more pronounced This paper explores the significance of Analysis of Variance ANOVA as a critical tool for understanding the relationships among multiple groups in various fields including healthcare economics and social sciences We provide a comprehensive review of ANOVAs evolution elucidating its foundational principles and recent advancements in computational techniques that enhance its applicability in contemporary research Additionally we discuss the increasing necessity for sound statistical inference due to the rising incidence of big data and the challenges posed by highdimensional datasets By illustrating realworld applications we demonstrate how ANOVA not only facilitates insights into group differences but also informs decisionmaking processes in policy formulation and scientific inquiry Our findings underscore that despite the emergence of novel statistical methods ANOVA remains an indispensable technique that aids researchers in navigating the complexities of modern data analysis This paper advocates for a renewed emphasis on ANOVA training and application ensuring future scholars are wellequipped to tackle the analytical demands of their disciplines

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we explore the effectiveness of redundant parameterizations in fitting hierarchical models which are widely used in various fields such as psychology ecology and economics to account for nested data structures Traditional approaches often struggle with convergence and identifiability issues particularly in complex models with multiple levels of variation We propose a novel framework that leverages redundant parameterizations to enhance model fitting and estimation stability Our methodology involves introducing additional noninformative parameters that facilitate the exploration of the parameter space thereby improving convergence rates and reducing sensitivity to initial conditions Through comprehensive simulations and realworld data applications we demonstrate that our approach yields superior estimation accuracy and robust inference compared to conventional methods Furthermore we provide guidelines for implementation including best practices for selecting redundant parameters and evaluating model performance This study not only offers a practical solution to challenges in hierarchical modeling but also contributes to the theoretical understanding of parameterization in complex models Our findings underscore the potential of redundant parameterizations as a powerful tool in statistical modeling paving the way for more flexible and reliable analyses of hierarchical data

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractExploratory Data Analysis EDA plays a pivotal role in the initial stages of datadriven research facilitating insights through visual and quantitative methods This paper proposes a novel Bayesian framework for EDA that integrates goodnessoffit testing to enhance the interpretation and analysis of complex datasets Our approach leverages Bayesian principles to quantify uncertainty allowing researchers to derive probabilistic insights into data distributions and model fit We introduce several Bayesian EDA techniques including posterior predictive checks Bayesian model comparison and credibility intervals which offer robust alternatives to traditional frequentist methods Through simulations and realworld examples we demonstrate that our Bayesian formulation not only provides clearer insights into data characteristics but also improves the reliability of goodnessoffit assessments This work advocates for a paradigm shift in EDA practices by incorporating Bayesian methods fostering a more nuanced understanding of data and models in statistical analysis
