text: A good choice of the proposal distribution is crucial for the rapid convergence of the Metropolis algorithm In this paper given a family of parameteric Markovian kernels we develop an adaptive algorithm for selecting the best kernel that maximizes the expected squared jumped distance an objective function that characterizes the Markov chain We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method In several examples

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIterative simulations are foundational in various fields including statistics machine learning and computational science Monitoring the convergence of these simulations is crucial to ensure reliable inference and decisionmaking This paper presents a comprehensive framework for assessing the convergence of iterative simulations which encompasses both frequentist and Bayesian approaches We introduce a set of general methodologies that leverage statistical tools such as diagnostic plots convergence metrics and predictive checks to evaluate the stability and consistency of simulation outputs over time Our methods are designed to accommodate a variety of simulation algorithms and models providing a flexible basis for practitioners We illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods through a series of simulation studies and realworld applications The results demonstrate that our framework can effectively identify convergence issues thereby enhancing the robustness and credibility of simulationbased analyses By providing a standardized approach to convergence monitoring we aim to contribute to best practices in iterative simulation methodologies fostering greater transparency and reliability in computational research

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Analysis of variance ANOVA is an extremely important method in exploratory and confirmatory data analysis Unfortunately in complex problems eg splitplot designs it is not always easy to set up an appropriate ANOVA We propose a hierarchical analysis that automatically gives the correct ANOVA comparisons even in complex scenarios The inferences for all means and variances are performed under a model with a separate batch of effects for each row of the ANOVA table We connect to classical ANOVA by working with finitesample variance components fixed and random effects models are characterized by inferences about existing levels of a factor and new levels respectively We also introduce a new graphical display showing inferences about the standard deviations of each batch of effects We illustrate with two examples from our applied data analysis first illustrating the usefulness of our hierarchical computations and displays and second showing how the ideas of ANOVA are helpful in understanding a previously fit hierarchical model

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Exploratory data analysis EDA and Bayesian inference or more generally complex statistical modelingwhich are generally considered as unrelated statistical paradigmscan be particularly effective in combination In this paper we present a Bayesian framework for EDA based on posterior predictive checks We explain how posterior predictive simulations can be used to create reference distributions for EDA graphs and how this approach resolves some theoretical problems in Bayesian data analysis We show how the generalization of Bayesian inference to include replicated data yrep and replicated parameters thetarep follows a long tradition of generalizations in Bayesian theory On the theoretical level we present a predictive Bayesian formulation of goodnessoffit testing distinguishing between pvalues posterior probabilities that specified antisymmetric discrepancy measures will exceed and uvalues data summaries with uniform sampling distributions We explain that pvalues unlike uvalues are Bayesian probability statements in that they condition on observed data Having reviewed the general theoretical framework we discuss the implications for statistical graphics and exploratory data analysis with the goal being to unify exploratory data analysis with more formal statistical methods based on probability models We interpret various graphical displays as posterior predictive checks and discuss how Bayesian inference can be used to determine reference distributions The goal of this work is not to downgrade descriptive statistics or to suggest they be replaced by Bayesian modeling but rather to suggest how exploratory data analysis fits into the probabilitymodeling paradigm We conclude with a discussion of the implications for practical Bayesian inference In particular we anticipate that Bayesian software can be generalized to draw simulations of replicated data and parameters from their posterior predictive distribution and these can in turn be used to calibrate EDA graphs

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Hierarchical linear and generalized linear models can be fit using Gibbs samplers and Metropolis algorithms these models however often have many parameters and convergence of the seemingly most natural Gibbs and Metropolis algorithms can sometimes be slow We examine solutions that involve reparameterization and overparameterization We begin with parameter expansion using working parameters a strategy developed for the EM algorithm This strategy can lead to algorithms that are much less susceptible to becoming stuck near zero values of the variance parameters than are more standard algorithms Second we consider a simple rotation of the regression coefficients based on an estimate of their posterior covariance matrix This leads to a Gibbs algorithm based on updating the transformed parameters one at a time or a Metropolis algorithm with vector jumps either of these algorithms can perform much better in terms of total CPU time than the two standard algorithms oneatatime updating of untransformed parameters or vector updating using a linear regression at each step We present an innovative evaluation of the algorithms in terms of how quickly they can get away from remote areas of parameter space along with some more standard evaluation of computation and convergence speeds We illustrate our methods with examples from our applied work Our ultimate goal is to develop a fast and reliable method for fitting a hierarchical linear model as easily as one can now fit a nonhierarchical model and to increase understanding of Gibbs samplers for hierarchical models in general

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Researchers sometimes argue that statisticians have little to contribute when few realizations of the process being estimated are observed We show that this argument is incorrect even in the extreme situation of estimating the probabilities of events so rare that they have never occurred We show how statistical forecasting models allow us to use empirical data to improve inferences about the probabilities of these events Our application is estimating the probability that your vote will be decisive in a US presidential election a problem that has been studied by political scientists for more than two decades The exact value of this probability is of only minor interest but the number has important implications for understanding the optimal allocation of campaign resources whether states and voter groups receive their fair share of attention from prospective presidents and how formal rational choice models of voter behavior might be able to explain why people vote at all We show how the probability of a decisive vote can be estimated empirically from statelevel forecasts of the presidential election and illustrate with the example of Based on generalizations of standard political science forecasting models we estimate the prospective probability of a single vote being decisive as about in million for close national elections such as varying by about a factor of among states Our results support the argument that subjective probabilities of many types are best obtained through empirically based statistical prediction models rather than solely through mathematical reasoning We discuss the implications of our findings for the types of decision analyses used in public choice studies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We describe a general approach using Bayesian analysis for the estimation of parameters in physiological pharmacokinetic models The chief statistical difficulty in estimation with these models is that any physiological model that is even approximately realistic will have a large number ofparameters often comparable to the number of observations in a typical pharmacokinetic experiment eg measurements and parameters for each subject In addition the parameters are generally poorly identified akin to the wellknown illconditioned problem of estimating a mixture of declining exponentials Our modeling includes a hierarchical population modeling which allows partial pooling of information among different experimental subjects b a pharmacokinetic model including compartments for wellperfused tissues poorly perfused tissues fat and the liver and c informative prior distributions for population parameters which is possible because the parameters represent real physiological variables We discuss how to estimate the models using Bayesian posterior simulation a method that automatically includes the uncertainty inherent in estimating such a large number of parameters We also discuss how to check model fit and sensitivity to the prior distribution using posterior predictive simulation We illustrate the application to the toxicokinetics of tetrachloroethylene perchloroethylene PERC the problem that motivated this work

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Title Estimating The Probability Of Events That Have Never Occurred When Is Your Vote Decisive In the realm of decision theory and electoral participation understanding the likelihood of events that have never previously transpired poses significant challenges for statisticians and voters alike This paper introduces a novel framework for estimating the probability of decisiveness in voting scenarios particularly in elections where historical data is sparse or nonexistent We employ advanced statistical techniques including Bayesian inference and nonparametric methods to evaluate the potential impact of an individuals vote in various electoral systems Through simulations and case studies we explore factors such as voter turnout margin of victory and system dynamics to derive a quantitative measure of decisiveness Our findings reveal crucial insights into when a single vote can alter the outcome providing voters with a clearer understanding of their influence in democratic processes This research not only enriches the theoretical landscape of decisionmaking under uncertainty but also offers practical implications for civic engagement and electoral strategy

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for conducting diagnostic checks in discrete data regression models through the application of posterior predictive simulations We investigate the efficacy of these simulations in assessing model fit and identifying potential model misspecifications in a variety of common discrete data scenarios including binary count and ordinal outcomes By leveraging Bayesian methodologies we generate posterior predictive distributions that allow us to compare observed data against predicted values enabling a robust evaluation of model adequacy A series of diagnostic tools such as predictive checks residual analysis and goodnessoffit measures are introduced and applied to both simulated datasets and realworld examples Our findings demonstrate that posterior predictive simulations not only provide substantial insights into the reliability of discrete regression models but also facilitate informed decisions in model selection and refinement processes Ultimately this work underscores the importance of incorporating rigorous diagnostic techniques in the analysis of discrete data promoting more accurate and interpretable statistical inferences

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of multilevel decision trees MLDTs as a method for classification and regression tasks in various domains We investigate the structural benefits and performance implications of employing multilevel decision trees compared to traditional singlelevel decision trees Our approach involves simulating multiple datasets that reflect varying characteristics in terms of dimensionality feature interaction and noise levels We perform an extensive set of experiments to compare MLDTs with other common algorithms such as random forests and support vector machines focusing on accuracy interpretability and computational efficiency The evaluation metrics include classification accuracy mean squared error and F score across diverse application scenarios including medical diagnostics financial forecasting and marketing analytics Results indicate that MLDTs not only provide improved predictive performance but also enhance model interpretability through their hierarchical structure Furthermore we analyze the robustness of MLDTs under different data conditions revealing their increased resilience to overfitting when compared to their singlelevel counterparts Our findings contribute to the advancement of decision tree methodologies and underscore the potential of MLDTs as a versatile tool in the statistical learning toolkit

author: Andrew Gelman
text: This paper investigates the phenomenon of incumbency advantage in electoral contexts through the lens of a beforeafter study design We employ a robust statistical framework to estimate the incumbency effect on electoral outcomes analyzing data from a series of electoral cycles across various jurisdictions Our methodology incorporates both fixed and random effects models to account for unobserved heterogeneity and temporal trends We delve into the variability of incumbency advantage across different political environments and demographic settings providing insights into factors that mediate this advantage The findings highlight significant variations in incumbency effects contingent on electoral competitiveness district characteristics and candidate attributes Additionally we discuss the implications of our results for electoral strategy and political science theory ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of incumbency dynamics in democratic elections By illuminating the nuances of incumbency advantage and its variations our study serves as a vital resource for policymakers political analysts and scholars alike paving the way for future research in this domain

author: Andrew Gelman
text: The evaluation of decision trees under uncertainty is difficult because of the required nested operations of maximizing and averaging Pure maximizing for deterministic decision trees or pure averaging for probability trees are both relatively simple because the maximum of a maximum is a maximum and the average of an average is an average But when the two operators are mixed no simplification is possible and one must evaluate the maximization and averaging operations in a nested fashion following the structure of the tree Nested evaluation requires large sample sizes for data collection or long computation times for simulations An alternative to full nested evaluation is to perform a random sample of evaluations and use statistical methods to perform inference about the entire tree We show that the most natural estimate is biased and consider two alternatives the parametric bootstrap and hierarchical Bayes inference We explore the properties of these inferences through a simulation study c Elsevier BV

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We investigate the construction of more precise estimates of a collection of population means using information about a related variable in the context of repeated sample surveys The method is illustrated using poll results concerning presidential approval rating our related variable is political party identification We use poststratification to construct these improved estimates but because we do not have population level information on the poststratifying variable we construct a model for the manner in which the poststratifier develops over time In this manner we obtain more precise estimates without making possibly untenable assumptions about the dynamics of our variable of interest the presidential approval rating

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Model checking with discrete data regressions can be difficult because the usual methods such as residual plots have complicated reference distributions that depend on the parameters in the model Posterior predictive checks have been proposed as a Bayesian way to average the results of goodnessoffit tests in the presence of uncertainty in estimation of the parameters We try this approach using a variety of discrepancy variables for generalized linear models fitted to a historical data set on behavioural learning We then discuss the general applicability of our findings in the context of a recent applied example on which we have worked We find that the following discrepancy variables work well in the sense of being easy to interpret and sensitive to important model failures structured displays of the entire data set general discrepancy variables based on plots of binned or smoothed residuals versus predictors and specific discrepancy variables created on the basis of the particular concerns arising in an application Plots of binned residuals are especially easy to use because their predictive distributions under the model are sufficiently simple that model checks can often be made implicitly The following discrepancy variables did not work well scatterplots of latent residuals defined from an underlying continuous model and quantilequantile plots of these residuals

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In an era characterized by data proliferation and complexity the importance of robust statistical methodologies has never been more pronounced This paper explores the significance of Analysis of Variance ANOVA as a critical tool for understanding the relationships among multiple groups in various fields including healthcare economics and social sciences We provide a comprehensive review of ANOVAs evolution elucidating its foundational principles and recent advancements in computational techniques that enhance its applicability in contemporary research Additionally we discuss the increasing necessity for sound statistical inference due to the rising incidence of big data and the challenges posed by highdimensional datasets By illustrating realworld applications we demonstrate how ANOVA not only facilitates insights into group differences but also informs decisionmaking processes in policy formulation and scientific inquiry Our findings underscore that despite the emergence of novel statistical methods ANOVA remains an indispensable technique that aids researchers in navigating the complexities of modern data analysis This paper advocates for a renewed emphasis on ANOVA training and application ensuring future scholars are wellequipped to tackle the analytical demands of their disciplines

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we explore the effectiveness of redundant parameterizations in fitting hierarchical models which are widely used in various fields such as psychology ecology and economics to account for nested data structures Traditional approaches often struggle with convergence and identifiability issues particularly in complex models with multiple levels of variation We propose a novel framework that leverages redundant parameterizations to enhance model fitting and estimation stability Our methodology involves introducing additional noninformative parameters that facilitate the exploration of the parameter space thereby improving convergence rates and reducing sensitivity to initial conditions Through comprehensive simulations and realworld data applications we demonstrate that our approach yields superior estimation accuracy and robust inference compared to conventional methods Furthermore we provide guidelines for implementation including best practices for selecting redundant parameters and evaluating model performance This study not only offers a practical solution to challenges in hierarchical modeling but also contributes to the theoretical understanding of parameterization in complex models Our findings underscore the potential of redundant parameterizations as a powerful tool in statistical modeling paving the way for more flexible and reliable analyses of hierarchical data

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In this paper we explore the concept of Predictive Information Criteria PIC within the framework of Bayesian modeling offering a comprehensive analysis of their role in model selection and evaluation With the increasing complexity of Bayesian models selecting an appropriate model becomes crucial and standard likelihoodbased approaches often fall short in addressing model uncertainty We introduce a systematic framework for understanding various PICs such as the Widely Applicable Information Criterion WAIC and the LeaveOneOut CrossValidation LOOCV elucidating their theoretical underpinnings and computational implementations Through extensive simulations and realworld applications we evaluate the performance of these criteria in different modeling scenarios highlighting their strengths and limitations Our findings demonstrate that while diverse PICs can yield similar rankings of models their predictive performance may significantly diverge thus necessitating careful consideration of the context in which they are utilized This work not only clarifies misconceptions surrounding predictive information criteria but also provides practical guidance for researchers engaging with Bayesian model selection We conclude by proposing recommendations for future research directions and the development of more robust criteria that can enhance predictive accuracy in complex Bayesian frameworks

author: Andrew Gelman
text: In the field of survey sampling poststratification is a powerful technique that enables researchers to adjust survey estimates to align with known population characteristics However traditional methods often rely on detailed populationlevel information about the poststratifying variable which can be unavailable or difficult to obtain This paper presents a novel approach to poststratification that circumvents the need for such populationlevel data by leveraging auxiliary information and statistical modeling techniques We develop a framework that integrates machine learning methods with traditional survey analysis to predict the distribution of the poststratifying variable within the target population Our approach is validated through a case study focused on political polling where conventional poststratification techniques have struggled to accommodate missing demographic data By applying this method to realworld polling data we demonstrate improvements in the accuracy of election forecasts and public opinion estimates The implications of this work extend to various fields where poststratification is employed offering a robust alternative for researchers facing challenges associated with incomplete population data We conclude with recommendations for practitioners on implementing this approach in future survey designs and analyses

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Hierarchical linear and generalized linear models can be fit using Gibbs samplers and Metropolis algorithms these models however often have many parameters and convergence of the seemingly most natural Gibbs and Metropolis algorithms can sometimes be slow We examine solutions that involve reparameterization and overparameterization We begin with parameter expansion using working parameters a strategy developed for the EM algorithm This strategy can lead to algorithms that are much less susceptible to becoming stuck near zero values of the variance parameters than are more standard algorithms Second we consider a simple rotation of the regression coefficients based on an estimate of their posterior covariance matrix This leads to a Gibbs algorithm based on updating the transformed parameters one at a time or a Metropolis algorithm with vector jumps either of these algorithms can perform much better in terms of total CPU time than the two standard algorithms oneatatime updating of untransformed parameters or vector updating using a linear regression at each step We present an innovative evaluation of the algorithms in terms of how quickly they can get away from remote areas of parameter space along with some more standard evaluation of computation and convergence speeds We illustrate our methods with examples from our applied work Our ultimate goal is to develop a fast and reliable method for fitting a hierarchical linear model as easily as one can now fit a nonhierarchical model and to increase understanding of Gibbs samplers for hierarchical models in general

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Analysis of variance ANOVA is an extremely important method in exploratory and confirmatory data analysis Unfortunately in complex problems eg splitplot designs it is not always easy to set up an appropriate ANOVA We propose a hierarchical analysis that automatically gives the correct ANOVA comparisons even in complex scenarios The inferences for all means and variances are performed under a model with a separate batch of effects for each row of the ANOVA table We connect to classical ANOVA by working with finitesample variance components fixed and random effects models are characterized by inferences about existing levels of a factor and new levels respectively We also introduce a new graphical display showing inferences about the standard deviations of each batch of effects We illustrate with two examples from our applied data analysis first illustrating the usefulness of our hierarchical computations and displays and second showing how the ideas of ANOVA are helpful in understanding a previously fit hierarchical model

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn the realm of survey research incomplete data poses significant challenges to accurate inference and decisionmaking This study introduces a novel multiple imputation framework specifically designed for handling nonresponse across multiple surveys where certain key questions remain unasked for subsets of participants We examine the implications of this selective nonresponse on the validity of statistical estimates and the potential biases introduced in subsequent analyses Our method leverages a combination of machine learning algorithms and hierarchical modeling to exploit the structure inherent in multiple datasets enabling the generation of plausible values for missing responses Through a comprehensive simulation study we validate our approach against traditional imputation methods highlighting improvements in estimation accuracy and robustness We further illustrate the practical application of our technique with realworld survey data demonstrating its efficacy in addressing complex patterns of nonresponse The results underscore the importance of advanced imputation methods in enhancing the reliability of survey findings ultimately contributing to more informed policy and research outcomes

author: Andrew Gelman
text: AbstractIn the realm of pharmacokinetics understanding the variability in drug response among individuals is crucial for optimizing therapeutic strategies This paper presents a comprehensive approach to physiological pharmacokinetic analysis by integrating population modeling with informative prior distributions We develop a hierarchical modeling framework that leverages rich clinical data to capture interindividual variability in drug absorption distribution metabolism and elimination processes Informative priors derived from previous studies and physiological benchmarks are employed to enhance parameter estimation and improve model robustness Utilizing a Bayesian inference framework we demonstrate how this approach facilitates the identification of demographic and physiological covariates that significantly influence pharmacokinetic parameters Our results indicate that the combination of population modeling with informative priors yields more accurate predictions of drug behavior across diverse patient populations The findings underscore the potential for this methodology to inform personalized medicine by enabling tailored dosing strategies that account for individual variability ultimately improving treatment outcomes in clinical settings

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We present a method of analyzing a series of independent crosssectional surveys in which some questions are not answered in some surveys and some respondents do not answer some of the questions posed The method is also applicable to a single survey in which different questions are asked or different sampling methods are used in different strata or clusters Our method involves multiply imputing the missing items and questions by adding to existing methods of imputation designed for single surveys a hierarchical regression model that allows covariates at the individual and survey levels Information from survey weights is exploited by including in the analysis the variables on which the weights were based and then reweighting individual responses observed and imputed to estimate population quantities We also develop diagnostics for checking the fit of the imputation model based on comparing imputed data to nonimputed data We illustrate with the example that motivated this project a study of preelection public opinion polls in which not all the questions of interest are asked in all the surveys so that it is infeasible to impute within each survey separately

author: Andrew Gelman
text: Incumbency advantage is one of the most widely studied features in American legislative elections In this article we construct and implement an estimate that allows incumbency advantage to vary between individual incumbents This model predicts that openseat elections will be less variable than those with incumbents running an observed empirical pattern that is not explained by previous models We apply our method to the US House of Representatives in the twentieth century Our estimate of the overall pattern of incumbency advantage over time is similar to previous estimates although slightly lower and we also find a pattern of increasing variation More generally our multilevel model represents a new method for estimating effects in beforeafter studies

author: Andrew Gelman
text: We review the Akaike deviance and WatanabeAkaike information criteria from a Bayesian perspective where the goal is to estimate expected outofsampleprediction error using a biascorrected adjustment of withinsample error We focus on the choices involved in setting up these measures and we compare them in three simple examples one theoretical and two applied The contribution of this paper is to put all these information criteria into a Bayesian predictive context and to better understand through small examples how these methods can apply in practice
